t: Leaders Who Manage Others Poorly by Email
q: Because it lacks the social, visual, and nonverbal cues essential for understanding, email is often misunderstood, misinterpreted, and overanalyzed.
That’s why email is such a terrible medium through which to express anything symbolic or humanly important. It leaves way too much to chance.
Instead, the medium allows people to drop “bombs” and then walk away without needing to deal with the consequences.
In fact, it is common for those leaders reliant on email to blast out negative group messages that should have targeted one or two team members. In such cases, everyone feels accused and reprimanded.
They know that nothing can replace the impact and clarity of face-to-face interaction, and they lead accordingly.
x: Because it strips out social and nonverbal cues, email invites over-interpretation from readers and, on the writer's side, encourages a more inflammatory tone than face-to-face conversation would allow.
Identifies a specific failure mode: sending group emails with negative feedback meant for one or two people, leaving everyone feeling accused.

t: What If Students Get Too Personal?
q: We want our students to know that we care — and to help with that, we need to actually care — but then again, our sanity and time constraints require us to keep the job of "teacher" from taking on too much of the jobs of "counselor" or "parent.
I've noticed a growing "sense" for when a student-teacher relationship is becoming too personal.
If a student does bring up these kinds of extra-personal, thorny topics, I like to ask things like, "Do you have anyone you can talk to about this?

If a student ever shares something super heavy (e.g., thoughts of self-harm, intense depression or anxiety, unsafe home), I get the student connected with the proper folks ASAP (e.g., counselor, admin, social worker, etc.).
It's a gentle but firm assertion of a boundary that I need in order to not bring work home, which is very important to me.

He credits eighteen years of experience with developing a felt "sense" for when a relationship is drifting too personal, acknowledging there's no formula, only accumulated judgment.
For students who do bring up heavy topics, his go-to redirect — "Do you have anyone you can talk to about this?" — signals connector rather than confidant without shutting the student down.
He draws a hard line at safety-relevant disclosures (self-harm, intense depression, unsafe home), routing those immediately to counselors, admin, or social workers rather than handling them himself.
He frames these as gentle but firm signals of a professional line rather than coldness, aimed at protecting both his capacity to teach well and his own boundaries against bringing work home.

t: Cultivating the Image of a Sage
q: They only enter the fray when they have something very special to say. Because what they offer is usually different and insightful, people get quiet when they speak.
Don’t be fooled. These colleagues are not shy or introverted. They intentionally choose not to say much unless their message will have a profound impact on others.
But they rob the team of their everyday input. By choosing not to engage as ideas develop, they allow the team to wander and find their way without their help.
The tagline, “When E.F. Hutton talks, people listen,” captured this idea to the delight of a generation of television consumers.
Good leaders don’t allow sages to climb the mountain. They insist on hearing what they have to say as the dialogue unfolds.

t: 'Growth mindset for teachers?'
q: Many critics argue that growth mindset has been reduced to slogans or used superficially - think the glossy poster on the corridor, rather than being embedded in high-quality teaching and learning strategies. Essentially, laminated, not lived.

A 2019 large randomised controlled trial involving over 12,000 students in the U.S. found only modest gains, mostly for lower-achieving students. A Meta-analysis revealed that growth mindset interventions often produce very small effects on academic outcomes, and sometimes none at all.

If you have a fixed mindset, feedback is unwelcome, because it might tell you are not as smart as you thought you were. If you have a growth mindset, feedback helps you maximise your improvement, by focusing your improvement on the things that are most likely to improve you.
Cognitive Coaching, developed by Costa and Garmston, emphasises the importance of guiding teachers to become self-directed learners by exploring their cognitive processes.

Through questioning, reframing negative thoughts and discussing decisions, instructional coaches can help teachers replace self-defeating thoughts with realistic, empowering solutions, leading to stronger resilience.

t: Research Bite #22: Cognitive Endurance as Human Capital
q: The authors conduct a field experiment with Indian primary school students, randomly assigning them to either sustained cognitive practice (using math problems or non-academic games) or a control group.

The study finds that both types of cognitive practice significantly improve cognitive endurance, as measured by reduced performance decline over time on various tests, and increase attentiveness in the classroom and school performance.

These effects are partially sustained even after a long break, and are complemented by quasi-experimental evidence showing that additional schooling improves cognitive endurance primarily in higher-quality schools.

The sources show that disadvantaged students experience cognitive fatigue more quickly than their more advantaged peers. Teachers can implement strategies to mitigate fatigue, such as incorporating short breaks or varying the types of activities.
The study shows that the positive impacts of schooling on cognitive endurance are concentrated in better quality schools, and those that assign more independent practice in class.
This indicates that the experience of effortful thinking itself—even when devoid of any subject content—increases the ability to accumulate traditional human capital

t: Leaders Who Add Too Much Value
q: But in their enthusiasm to influence others with their insights, leaders can sometimes go too far. They can add too much value and throw a wrench into the discussion that isn’t always obvious to them.

By being quick to offer too many ideas, suggestions, and options, they undermine the contributions of others, discourage those with less experience from sharing their ideas, and make decision-making much more complex than it needs to be.
Coaching these leaders and team members to allow others to speak first can help them understand the negative impact they normally have on discussions.
The urge to contribute their ideas and suggestions in every discussion, even when it’s unnecessary, usually springs from a combination of self-confidence and the need to control outcomes.
Convincing those with this affliction that a leader’s job is to highlight everyone else’s ideas so they can grow and develop can start a personal transformation.
x: This essay addresses passionate, knowledgeable leaders who unintentionally dominate meetings by contributing too many ideas, options, and suggestions.

t: Why You Need A Student Leadership Team
q: Every year, I ask three or four students with natural leadership ability to be part of my leadership team.

It’s important to mention that “leadership” doesn’t necessarily mean the best or most well-behaved students. These traits are irrelevant. I look for those with the most influence with their classmates.
Typically, this will include at least one difficult or challenging student. In fact, the most insightful input often comes from kids with the worst reputations on campus.
Yes, they will, but only if you’re consistently kind and clam and a stickler about enforcing rules. Do this and they’ll tell you everything .
There is one more benefit of having a leadership team, and it may be the most important one of all. The members of your team will start proactively using their influence for good.

They’ll naturally begin acting as your proxy, representing, modeling, and channeling your kindness, fairness, and high standards during group work, while listening to lessons, and even out on the playground.

t: Leaders Raised by Wolves
q: It’s somewhat astounding how often leaders who play favorites, manage work-life balance poorly, have difficulty delegating to others, and express high emotions when they are frustrated have experienced those same tactics themselves from a leader or role model in their lives.
The odds are that if a leader had a previous manager or mentor who was a micromanager, they, too, resort to this coercive style.
Micromanagers in any industry or workplace share a common set of tactics. First and foremost, they presume team members are incapable of completing tasks without detailed guidance and supervision.
Of course, the real explanation is that the mentor succeeded despite their micromanaging, which means they had a lot of luck in the process or had such extreme talent that they overwhelmed this flaw.
Celebrating the role models we have admired and learned from by emulating their behaviors is what good leaders do. But only after they reject those tactics that are ineffective or harmful.
x: Argues micromanagement is most often learned by imitation from a prior mentor or role model, not chosen out of a need for control.
Identifies the core reasoning error: assuming a mentor's micromanaging style caused their success rather than being survived despite it.
Catalogs specific micromanaging tactics — presumed incompetence, constant status demands, requiring approval for everything — and their team-level costs.

It argues people mistake correlation for causation — assuming a mentor's heavy-handed oversight caused their success, rather than recognizing the mentor succeeded despite that flaw, through luck or overwhelming talent.
Closes by urging leaders to consciously reject harmful inherited behaviors rather than emulate every trait of an admired mentor.

t: You Can Lead a Horse to Water…
q: Too often, I encounter students who believe they can simply sit, passively in a lesson and absorb what is being taught, without having to do anything.
I didn’t watch them to learn. I hadn’t put my brain in gear, I hadn’t engaged what needed to be engaged in order to learn it.
We have to force our students to put their brains into gear, we have to depress the clutch if you will.
Rather than jumping in with moles = mass ÷ relative formula mass, first we looked at Mr. We checked we could do that, then we looked at the concept of a mole and we checked we could do that.
By demanding, by expecting and sanctioning as appropriate, student participation in my lesson, I am making it more likely that they will get into gear and put their brain in learning mode.

When it comes to revision, when it comes to them assessing whether they know and understand something, get them answering questions rather than highlighting things. It's much harder to lie to yourself and convince yourself you know something when you're getting the questions wrong.

q: There are SO MANY issues that teachers have to think about every lesson just to run the room and work through the curriculum.
The key thing is not to just expect or hope for attention – it's to require it through the structure of your means of participation: cold calling, show-me boards, pair-share.
Ever since Oliver Caviglioli shared his view that cognitive load theory largely comes down to the problem of transience, I’ve noticed it in lessons over and over again.

It's actually remarkable how much students can do in this way without learning much: copy diagrams; write out worked examples; copy model paragraphs; create tables of information, 'borrow' answers from their neighbours.

t: The MGC Inflection Point
q: Here's what the resistance sounds like: I already do this. Why do I need to keep track? I don't have time to do this.
The good news is, it's an inflection point — a momentary pause in upward progress, a brief decline before another rise if you keep going.
It's an interaction with a student where you're TRYING TO COMMUNICATE that you value, know, or respect them. You have a main intention in the interaction: I see you. I respect you. I value you.
It's instead one of those moments where you go up to the kid and ask them how the game went last night. YOU thought of THEM.
They don't need to be LONG or AMAZING or DEEP. They just need to be intentional.

t: Teams That Reject a New Colleague
q: It is not uncommon for the newcomer to be disrespected, excluded, or ignored either openly or more subtly. This makes meetings and exchanges involving the new colleague awkward at best and hostile at worst.
That’s reasonable counsel but focused on the wrong party. The problem lies with the team, not the new colleague.

Good leaders lay out their clear expectations for integrating and acclimating any new colleague. They personally sit down with each team member and explain the value the new colleague can bring to the team.
To avoid having some team members ignore the new colleague, they often assign projects and tasks that require team members to interact and achieve outcomes with the new colleague.
Teams will sometimes give themselves permission to behave unprofessionally toward a new colleague if they think the leader will stand for it. Your job is never to stand for it.
x: Insists new colleagues must never be excluded from meetings, email chains, or conversations as a baseline standard.
Frames team rejection of a new colleague as a leadership failure of standard-setting, not an inevitable social friction to be waited out.

It rejects the standard advice of telling the new colleague to be patient and build relationships one at a time, insisting instead that leaders must set explicit expectations for how existing team members treat the…

t: Seeking Disconfirming Information About a Proposed Decision Will Elevate Conviction, Not Diminish It
q: Leaders and team members are naturally prone to seek information that confirms their existing beliefs. And ignore evidence that contradicts their views.
To counteract this bias, good leaders actively seek disconfirming information to create a more balanced and objective view.

The reason is straightforward: After exposing the weaknesses and false assumptions of a prospective decision, if the proposal still remains attractive to the team, it means the decision is exemplary and highly supported based upon an objective view.
They deliberately invite dissenting views, gather contrary evidence from external sources, and invite their own team members to raise challenges to the orthodoxy of the current view.
In the end, a decision that stands the test of scrutiny is likely to be the best choice. Good leaders always invite disagreement before reaching a sound conclusion.
x: This piece argues against a common fear that seeking out contrary evidence before a decision will slow things down and weaken team resolve.
Reframes the fear that disconfirming information slows decisions and weakens conviction as backwards — scrutiny actually strengthens legitimate decisions.
Argues confirmation bias, left unchecked, blinds teams to a false or incomplete picture of reality.
Positions the leader's core responsibility as actively inviting dissent and gathering external contrary evidence, not just tolerating disagreement when it arises.

t: Every Student Known
q: One of the biggest challenges I face when doing PD around the country and world is helping folks think hard about basic strategies like this one.

In a survey to our students, they were given a chance to name an educator they felt they had a connection with. What blew me away is that every single professional in our building was named by at least one student.
And what did it take? A few dozen clipboards and dogged persistence. Good faith efforts — not perfect ones — through good days and bad.
You can't do MGCs just like I do. And I can't do them like you do. But we can both keep track.
This is all that it took for our team to accomplish what none of us could have accomplished independently — every kid with a connection, and every adult named by at least one kid.

t: Closing in on Success, Performers Crave Near-Win Feedback
q: When performers, athletes, or team members almost achieve a desired outcome but fall just short, it is critical for leaders to provide just the right feedback that will inspire greater effort for the next performance.

Good leaders are not shy about reminding team members and teams when they are tremendously close to success. They point out the likelihood of the desired outcome and get specific as to what stands in the way.
Your proposal was well-received and missed by only one vote. Once you further refine your outline and practice prior to presenting, you will win the contract.
The role of the leader in facilitating this “Near-Win Effect” is to direct their attention toward exactly what improvement or change will make the difference.

Counterintuitively, it is not always essential that the leader know exactly what will propel the team or team members forward. Great leaders know that the real victory is in believing, and they do their part to amplify that conviction.
x: Claims performers are unusually receptive to feedback in this window, making it a high-leverage coaching moment.
Recommends replacing generic praise with specific feedback naming exactly what stands between a performer and success.

It closes with the counterintuitive claim that a leader doesn't need to know the precise fix; simply reinforcing belief in imminent success is often what propels performers forward.

t: Research Bite #21: Teaching with Worked Examples
q: The authors argue that the choice of problems influences the ambiguity of the resulting examples, with more ambiguous examples leading to poorer learning outcomes.
Four studies are presented, demonstrating that less ambiguous examples consistently resulted in better test performance, fewer misconceptions, and more accurate self-assessment of learning.
Even seemingly minor variations in the problem statement can affect the ambiguity of the worked example, influencing students’ ability to understand the concept being taught.
Problems that lead to solutions that coincidentally include elements from the problem statement should be avoided, as they tend to be more ambiguous and can lead to misconceptions.
Teachers should be aware that students often prioritize learning from examples over explanations, even when provided with both.
The results confirm that the selection of problems to exemplify influences the ambiguity of worked examples and indicate that selecting problems that lead to MAE impair (meta)comprehension
x: Across four experiments, the authors show that even small differences in which problem is used to demonstrate a procedure can make the resulting worked example more or less ambiguous, and that more ambiguous examples…

Across four experiments, the authors show that even small differences in which problem is used to demonstrate a procedure can make the resulting worked example more or less ambiguous, and that more ambiguous examples…
The core finding that problem selection, not just explanation quality, drives whether a worked example teaches the right rule or an accidental wrong one.
Ambiguous examples -- where the solution coincidentally shares surface features with the problem statement -- are a specific, avoidable trap in item and example design.
Students systematically prioritize learning from the example itself over the accompanying explanation, meaning a bad example isn't reliably rescued by good verbal teaching.

The paper's practical constraint for time-pressed teachers: when only a few worked examples can be used, the selection of the specific problem deserves as much scrutiny as the explanation written around it.

t: Leaders Who Blame and Shame
q: Far too often, they engage in what is called Blame and Shame.
The Blame and Shame strategy can be highly effective on the short term or in an instance. Over the long term, however, it can erode trust and respect.

This is because accusation and embarrassment linger with team members for much longer than the admonishment. Moreover, team members build up a resistance to being confronted over performance if it happens too frequently.
When reminders and nudges don’t work to push the team and team members toward better execution, the better strategy is for the leader to engage in the task or assignment with them.
Good leaders use blame and shame sparingly, if at all. They work with team members to raise their standards and get the job done on time.
x: This piece critiques a common but corrosive corrective tactic: publicly calling out a team or individual for dropping the ball as a way to spur better effort.
'Blame and Shame' can produce short-term compliance but degrades trust and suppresses bad-news reporting over the long run.
Public accusation lingers with team members far longer than the moment of admonishment itself.
The recommended alternative is co-executing the task with the underperforming team member rather than simply demanding better results.

As an alternative, it recommends leaders work alongside underperforming team members on the task itself, using that shared effort to model standards and rebuild the relationship rather than simply demanding more.

t: When a Complete Baller Wont Talk About It
q: Each year, this mysterious man who plays Augusta National on the weekends as a member gets to play in the tournament without ever qualifying for the field. The Club doesn’t talk about him, and the broadcast crews are instructed not to show him on camera.
How did this stand-in do? Tom Kim, in his post-tournament press conference, called him a “complete baller,” which is another way of saying this guy can really play.

A CEO who can’t play the role of a Marker inside their own organization is probably not much of a Chief Executive. To act nothing more than a guy or gal standing in on some project or task is exactly what makes them worth following.
The best leaders act as a Marker on purpose at times to exercise this muscle and to show others that they are not above playing any role the organization needs.
The flexibility to sometimes be the outspoken leader and sometimes be the Marker doesn’t come naturally for anyone. It takes humility, confidence, and a knowledge of what leadership is all about.

t: Leaders Who Awkwardly Overshare About Themselves
q: Some leaders can’t stop themselves from disclosing too much. They make others feel awkward and uncomfortable whenever they share too many personal issues and details.

Leaders who tell others what they really think and feel about issues normally enhance their credibility. We like leaders who are more open and honest about what they think. But this doesn’t apply to their personal lives or deeply held suspicions or complaints.
As people pull away from them, they often feel the need to disclose even more to reestablish their connection. This can make conversations exasperating.
Team members can help leaders who overshare by validating the conversation and then abruptly changing the topic.

By abruptly shifting topics, those on the receiving end draw a boundary line that is difficult to breach. Over time, leaders learn that team members are uninterested in exploring such personal issues further.

t: Beware of Frenemies
q: A Frenemy refers to a person with whom one has a friendly or cordial relationship but who secretly harbors an underlying hostility and rivalry.
Frenemies appear to be supportive on the surface, but behind the water, they believe they are in competition with you and so must do their best to win.

Frenemies typically offer compliments but follow them with criticisms and veiled insults: “You did a great job. You must have had a lot of help.” Praise from a frenemy is always followed by a critical comment.
They pull you into situations and disputes to make you look bad: “I’m going to get you involved with a sticky issue because you’ll know just what to do.
Better that you know that they exist and work to circumvent their negative power by calling out their high jinks. When frenemies are exposed, they lose much of their influence.
x: Defines the 'frenemy' pattern as friendly surface behavior masking genuine rivalry and a desire to undermine.
This essay profiles the workplace 'frenemy' — someone who maintains a friendly facade while secretly competing to make a colleague look bad.
Lists concrete diagnostic phrases and behaviors — backhanded praise, comparison, conspicuous silence — that reveal a frenemy in action.
Frenemies frequently pull colleagues into disputes and later disclaim responsibility for the fallout.
The piece argues frenemies rely on the target's trust to stay effective, and that naming and exposing the pattern is the most reliable way to blunt their influence.

t: Using Identities to Elevate Team Member Engagement
q: To increase the odds that team members will embrace their calls for action with more vigor and enthusiasm, great leaders have learned a secret. They turn their requests for action into identities that people must live up to.
Consider the difference between describing someone as learning versus describing that person as a learner. The persona of a learner seems more permanent and more likely to persist.
For example, instead of asking a team member to innovate, they ask them to be an Innovator. Rather than ask them to be more decisive, they ask them to be the Decision-Maker.
As author and proponent of this idea, Jonah Berger likes to say, “Cheating is bad, but being a cheater is worse. Losing is bad, but being a loser is worse.
So, the next time you get in a jam, don’t ask a colleague to help you. Instead, ask them to be a “friend and pitch in.” You’ll likely find they lend a hand with a lot more enthusiasm.
x: Identities feel more permanent than actions, which is why people work harder to live up to them once named.

t: How to Woodenize Working Memory (Woodenization Example)
q: The trouble with working memory, I tell my students, is that it is limited. For everyone. No matter how smart you are, you've got less than a handful of chunks in working memory.
Picture your working memory as a small iceberg island, and each thing you're thinking about is a penguin. The island can only hold so many penguins. Add too many, and a penguin has to slip off.
It feels bad to overload your working memory, just like it feels bad to choke on too much food. This "choking" language is what Barbara Oakley uses in her bestselling A Mind for Numbers.
Systems of writing are THE greatest mind-expanding invention ever made by human beings. Whenever my students CAN take notes to keep penguins on the island, I tell them they SHOULD take notes.
This kind of work is pretty quick in the classroom, but what it's doing for the Effort and Efficacy (not to mention Credibility and Belonging) beliefs is not to be scoffed at.

t: How To Handle A Student Who Yells 'But I Didn't Do Anything!'
q: Such reaction is becoming more common because more students are growing up without being told no. In their mind, calling out in class or wandering the room or otherwise doing what they feel like isn’t “wrong.
Now, it’s important to note that schools are quick to label these children with ODD, CD, IED, ADHD, XYZ and the like. It’s not their fault, you see. They can’t help it, you see.

In the above scenario, the worst thing you can do—other than ignoring their misbehavior and accepting it as their disorder talking—is to repeat, remind, convince, explain, or argue why calling out is wrong.

Never, ever give in. Parents don’t care? Child doesn’t care? Call their bluff and follow through anyway. The magic isn’t in the consequences per se, it’s in your consistency and expert whole-class classroom management.
Because unwavering accountability sends a loud and clear message deep into the heart that you care. You refuse to give up on them, and are likely the only one.
You hold them to a standard because they have worth. They will feel this and know it to be true.

Never explain, argue, or individually justify the rule to the student, even under pressure from repeated protest.
Consistency itself is the message of care -- refusing to give in proves to the student that the teacher believes they're capable of better.

t: The Many Advantages of Pre-Planned Pauses
q: Pre-planned pauses are particularly useful for leaders to create strong transitions between topics, issues, and decisions during meetings.
By pausing between those distinct activities, leaders can prevent allowing tactics or solutions to contaminate their thinking about the problem or opportunity.
Properly timed, pauses deescalate conflict by interrupting heightened emotions and by allowing the parties the time they need to reflect and reset.

Leaders often think they can pause whenever they need to or call for it in process, and that is sometimes the case. But it can be awkward to request a timeout or to announce a cooling-off period during a moment of intensity.

As they design meetings, practices, decision debates, conflict mediations, offsites, and team discussions, good leaders think ahead and decide what intentional breaks in the action might prove highly valuable.
x: Pre-planned pauses prevent solution-thinking from contaminating problem diagnosis by creating a deliberate seam between the two activities.

t: What Leadership Transparency Really Means
q: Transparency is a very specific set of actions. Leaders who say they value transparency either prove it by their actions or they don’t.

First, they inform others quickly about decisions, initiatives, and changes but go beyond merely describing “what” is occurring. They make it a point to explain the “why” behind the differences they are putting in place.
Unfavorable data, like cost overruns or regulatory roadblocks, are discussed openly and are not hidden from view.
They don’t decide on their own whether the outcome was a success but seek feedback from those affected to arrive at this conclusion and then communicate that view.
Too many leaders think they are transparent when they are not. While it begins with being open and honest, that’s not enough.

t: Are Worksheets Bad?
q: But — but! — there are instances where things that look an awful lot like worksheets are simply the best and most efficient means through which to achieve a certain instructional goal.

The warm-ups will not work if you use them like worksheets. You can't just hand them out and let the kids go. I try to think of each warm-up as an interactive lesson with multiple checks for understanding.

But in the hands of an earnest teacher who takes the time to read the science and strategies behind this worksheet, this can become a recurring tool for creating pair, small group, and whole-class discussions around how Algebra or Physics or Hamlet or the Han Dynasty relates to students' actual lives.
There were practically tears by the end from multiple participants because it was so beautifully done.

Sweeping statements like "worksheets are the worst," "all books are good books," "desks in rows are terrible…" these provide the illusion of clarity (all over-generalizations do) but not clarity's substance.

t: Building Up Delegation Trust
q: Too many leaders hold onto tasks they don’t need to and thereby become less effective themselves while robbing team members of the necessary development challenges they need to grow.

The best leaders build delegation trust by first assigning smaller, less critical tasks to team members. They give themselves the chance to see the way team members approach these assignments, the attention to detail and quality they pursue, and the judgment they use to work through choices and challenges.
Debriefing these small tasks and assignments allows team members to learn what is expected of them in the future and gives leaders the chance to impart critical standards and values.
Some team members earn the delegation trust to take on the most significant tasks the leader faces, while others are relegated to smaller assignments and initiatives.
In short order, the adage “If you want something done right, you have to do it yourself” becomes replaced with the mindset “If you want to get everything done, you have to delegate.
x: Leaders who hoard tasks aren't protecting quality; they're diluting their own effectiveness and blocking team development.
Debriefing small delegated tasks is where leaders transmit standards, attention to detail, and judgment expectations to team members.

Trust compounds unevenly — some team members earn bigger assignments faster than others, and that's an expected part of the process.

t: Authenticity and Writing With Artificial Intelligence
q: But readers of those words will become increasingly concerned with their authenticity. When others know an artificial intelligence is used to compose your words, readers will naturally question the sincerity, authenticity, and originality of that writing.

But more personal messages, such as blog posts, personal letters, heartfelt expressions, advice, and requests for assistance (among many other symbolic messages) will be scrutinized and treated harshly if and when AI is used to create them.
People will soon increasingly seek out music, art, novels, and other forms of creative expression that originate directly from artists and that do not use AI.
Field Notes does not rely on AI for writing or editing. By design and choice. The words, as imperfect as they are, come from real people with deep experience.
Here's a good rule: If you would feel embarrassed or awkward if others were to learn you used AI to create a message, then you should avoid using it.

t: Resolving Wicked Problems
q: Wicked problems are complex and multi-faceted, with competing advocates that cannot escape engaging one another.

What makes a problem truly wicked isn’t just its complexity or competing choices. It is the potential for conflict and unintended relational consequences if one side were to be selected over the other.
The first step for the leader is to publicly acknowledge the complexity of the problem and how the competing sides both have a legitimate claim for selection.

Lastly and most importantly, the leader initiates Participatory Redesign. Rather than select one option over the other, they ask stakeholders and experts to explore what elements can be combined, used concurrently, or positioned for use with different audiences or times.
The only villain is the inflexibility that occurs when people are allowed to insist on their viewpoints without interruption.
x: Wicked problems are defined less by complexity than by the relational conflict that follows from choosing one side over another.

Participatory Redesign — combining elements of competing options rather than picking a winner — is presented as the ultimate resolution technique.

t: How To Handle Pesky, Advantageous Inattentiveness
q: Yet, the second you look away, even for a brief moment, you lose them and the momentum of your lesson. You’re able to bring them back, but it’s still frustrating.
It’s human nature. You see, whenever our attention is broken unexpectedly, we seek stimulation elsewhere. Think of being in a movie theater when the projector breaks.
This is why students start turning and looking around so quickly. They make eye contact with friends. They motion to each other. They side-talk or stare out the window.
The solution is to bring the issue out into the open. Unplanned pauses during lessons are going to happen. When they do, your students need to know exactly what is and isn’t okay.
To ensure the lesson is clear, you may want to be sneaky for a few days. Bluff, pretend, act as if you’re lost in thought or your attention is elsewhere and see if anyone side-talks.
This will strengthen their new habit, build academic discipline, and increase their ability to focus for longer and longer periods of time.

t: The Key to Reading Micro Expressions
q: Reading people is a prized leadership skill and critical for leadership success.
Micro expressions are the brief, involuntary facial expressions, lasting a fraction of a second, that reveal a person’s true emotions even when they’re trying to conceal them.
Research confirms that the emotions revealed by micro expressions are universal across cultures.
To better read micro expressions, practice by using them in a mirror.
Emotions not only cause facial expressions, but facial expressions also cause emotions.

t: Do You Truly Motivate or Just Bribe Others to Raise Their Game
q: Chief among the needs leaders tap into to compel action and inspire higher performance are incentives.
But here’s the irony, for decades research has shown that external rewards, such as compensation, actually diminish the natural and intrinsic motivation people have to do a better job.
Without realizing it, leaders who are too incentive-focused rob people of their intrinsic motivations.

Great leaders do their best to limit their use of incentives and authority to get things done because they know that long-term success depends on team members who are intrinsically motivated to reach for quality results.
No leader wants to think of themselves as bribing others to do their best, but that’s exactly what occurs in a workplace driven primarily through external rewards.

If you're trying to study, a distraction could be your phone, your little sibling, or your wandering thoughts about friends. If you're trying to enjoy time hanging out with your friends, a distraction could be your phone or your wandering thoughts about schoolwork.

Novice teachers, who often struggle to anticipate student needs due to limited experience, can particularly benefit from this approach.

t: Connecting Goals to Criticism Shows Others Youre Trying to Help and Not Hurt Them
q: People don’t separate the content of feedback from the person giving it.
For the feedback to land successfully, those on the receiving end must believe the giver is trying to make them better and improve their performance.
Because many leaders, parents, and coaches use feedback as a weapon to torment or wound others, people are on guard against negative intentions.
The best leaders do something remarkably simple to clarify their positive intentions: They tie the feedback to specific goals and outcomes before offering it.
And that’s always your goal with feedback—to change behavior or improve performance. Anything else is just catharsis — or worse.
x: Feedback is judged almost entirely through the perceived intent of the giver, not just the accuracy of the content.

Stating the specific goal or desired outcome before delivering feedback makes benevolent intent transparent more effectively than simply declaring good intentions.

t: The Country Club Mindset
q: Why are so many clubs, volunteer organizations, and member-centric associations so poorly run?
This means leaders take on a “Country Club” mindset, whereby anything that is not immediately connected to member satisfaction is given little attention.
The result is a relaxed and sometimes fun work environment where productivity suffers from a lack of direction and oversight.
Ask your club for the overall vision of the institution and the visions of each department.

t: For the Hopelessly Impatient
q: Impatient people simply can’t wait. They want to hear the news, achieve the outcome, and talk through the problem right NOW.
Self-regulation evaporates under the heat of urgent, excitable, or stressful situations.
Instead of slowing down and waiting for what they want to know, do, or achieve, cravenly impatient people need to speed up at something else.
The idea is not to fight your desire for impatience but to feed it.
Sometimes, using a weakness against itself makes us stronger.

t: Remembering What It's Like To Be A Student
q: It is so incredibly difficult to listen to a concept that you have little knowledge of, retain that information, and use it appropriately when needed…especially when you’ve only attended to that content once.
Sometimes we forget what it’s like to be a student. We forget what it’s like to sit in a classroom and experience terms and concepts that are totally new.
Teachers, or really anyone with a firm grasp of any particular domain of knowledge, are especially susceptible to displaying the curse of knowledge.
Humans are unfortunately vulnerable to assuming others have a shared foundation of knowledge and set expectations based on this bias.
Until your students have had numerous experiences hearing, seeing, and applying the material, should they be expected to know how to use it correctly? I'm not so sure.
Not only does this create an environment that normalizes forgetting and makes it acceptable to try and fail and try again, it also models for students more effective learning strategies.

t: How To Handle Your Students' Smart Phone Withdrawal
q: Since the advent of the smart phone, interest in acquiring academic skill and knowledge has dwindled.
Kids spend hour upon hour scrolling hits of dopamine and it’s crushed their desire to learn. Even worse, once their phones are put away for class, they go through withdrawal.
Great literature has been replaced with short articles and excerpts. Lessons are brief and include video, images, and interactive technology. Laptops are rarely out of sight and loosely monitored.
This has allowed students to skate by from one grade to the next, and even earn high marks with absurdly poor reading and writing skills.
Instead of shortening and increasing stimulation, we believe in doing the opposite: Slow down, provide great lessons, push the envelop on independent work, and heal their damaged brains.
Students appreciate and do better in a serious academic environment that will challenge them rather than one that capitulates to the jump-cut entertainment world and toxicity of social media.

t: How Are Others Interpreting What You Say and Do
q: A popular maxim among communication professionals is that people “cannot NOT communicate.
Of the many possible readings people make of your behavior, three stand out for their importance: task, identity, and relationship.
At the same time, the message or behavior also communicates and reinforces the identity or social image of the communicator.
The best communicators are thoughtful about the three interpretations others make and attempt to be mindful of doing things that convey how they want to be viewed.
Only messages that balance all three components have the potential to create the positive interpretations good people want and desire from others.

t: Know Your Worth
q: The value of expertise is uneven and hard to measure. Those with the experience, know-how, street smarts, and acumen to apply their knowledge to important problems and opportunities will always be in high demand.
As the story goes, the legendary artist Pablo Picasso was at a Paris restaurant when an admirer approached him and asked if he could do a quick sketch on a paper napkin.
The patron exclaimed, “40,000 francs! It only took you three minutes.” Picasso coolly replied, “No, it took me all my life.

q: Every leader wants a team of proactive colleagues who anticipate needs, issues, and opportunities and step up to address them without being asked.
People anticipate and take the initiative when two things exist: an expectation that they should do so, and recognition for being proactive even when the outcome of their effort is less than desired.

t: The Trouble With Sitting Behind Our Desks
q: The person who does the work does the learning; the mind changes through work as the body changes through work.

When we don't have independent work happening at all in our classrooms — choosing instead modes like direct instruction or collaborative learning — we run the risk of individual students avoiding the individual work it takes for a mind to learn.

If it becomes a habit, I run the risk of harming my Credibility with students. Even if I'm at work on something directly beneficial to them (e.g., feedback on their work), me habitually retreating to my desk while they work independently can send the signal that I'm detached from what they're doing.

t: Show Respect by Asking Others to Go First
q: Team members want a lot from their leader. They want to be heard, liked, valued, appreciated, and involved.
Savvy leaders who are acutely aware of the critical nature of respect do something less common but powerfully important to show their respect. They insist that others go first.
Listening to a team member before offering their own view is a unique sign of respect by a leader.
Letting others go first is a powerful way to demonstrate how much you appreciate and admire who they are.
Leaders who want to be heard listen to others (in many ways) first. Leaders give respect to receive it.
